key_points: Among laboratory tests, troponin is useful for detection of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in AHF, although elevated levels are detected in the vast majority of patients with AHF.
Blood urea nitrogen/urea, serum creatinine, electrolytes and antigen carbohydrate 125 may help tailor treatment.
Detection of abnormal liver function identifies patients with poor prognosis.
Since both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism may precipitate AHF, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) should be assessed in newly diagnosed AHF.
Arterial blood gas analysis should be done when precise measurement of O2 and CO2 partial pressure is needed (e.g., respiratory distress).
Lactate and pH should be measured in patients with cardiogenic shock.
D-dimer should be measured when acute pulmonary embolism is suspected.
Procalcitonin may be used for diagnosis of pneumonia; antibiotic therapy may be indicated when plasma levels are >0.2 µg/L.
Pulse oximetry should be measured routinely at first presentation of patients with AHF and continuous monitoring may be needed in the first hours or days.
content.section_summary: Four major clinical presentations of acute heart failure described based on signs of congestion and/or peripheral hypoperfusion and requiring different treatments.
